questions.q: An article bought for ₹500 is sold for ₹575. The profit percent is:
questions.e: Profit = 575 − 500 = ₹75. Profit % = 75/500 × 100 = 15%, always calculated on cost price.

questions.q: A shirt costing ₹800 is sold at a loss of 15%. Its selling price is:
questions.e: Loss = 15% of 800 = ₹120, so SP = 800 − 120 = ₹680. ₹120 is only the loss.

questions.sub: cost and selling price of articles
questions.q: If the cost price of 20 articles equals the selling price of 16 articles, the profit percent is:
questions.e: Let each article cost ₹1, so SP of 16 = ₹20 and SP of one = ₹1.25. Profit = 0.25 on ₹1, which is 25%.

questions.q: The marked price of a bag is ₹600 and a discount of 20% is allowed. The selling price is:
By selling an article for ₹750 a shopkeeper gains 25%. The cost price is:
questions.e: SP = 1.25 × CP, so CP = 750 ÷ 1.25 = ₹600. Taking 25% off 750 would give the wrong ₹562.50.

questions.q: An article is sold for ₹360 at a loss of 10%. Its cost price is:
A radio is bought for ₹80 and sold for ₹68. The loss percent is:
An item marked ₹800 is sold for ₹680. The rate of discount is:
questions.e: Discount = 800 − 680 = ₹120. Rate = 120/800 × 100 = 15% of the marked price.

questions.q: A trader buys goods for ₹2500 and sells them at a gain of 12%. The selling price is:
Two successive discounts of 20% and 10% are equal to a single discount of:
questions.e: Net factor = 0.8 × 0.9 = 0.72, so the single discount is 28%. Adding 20 + 10 = 30 is the usual slip.

questions.q: A shopkeeper marks his goods 40% above cost price and allows a discount of 20%. His profit percent is:
questions.e: Take CP = 100. MP = 140 and SP = 0.8 × 140 = 112. Profit = 12%.

questions.q: Two articles are sold for ₹1200 each, one at a gain of 20% and the other at a loss of 20%. On the whole the transaction results in:
questions.e: When two items are sold at the same price with equal gain and loss x%, there is always a loss of x²/100 % = 400/100 = 4%. Check: CP = 1000 + 1500 = 2500, SP = 2400, loss = 100 = 4%.

questions.sub: cost and selling price of articles
questions.q: The selling price of 15 articles equals the cost price of 18 articles. The gain percent is:
questions.e: Let each cost ₹1. Then SP of 15 = ₹18, so SP of one = ₹1.20. Gain = 20% of cost.

questions.q: A shopkeeper allows a 10% discount on the marked price and still makes a 20% profit. The marked price is what percent above the cost price?
questions.e: SP = 1.2 CP = 0.9 MP, so MP = 1.2/0.9 × CP = 4/3 CP. That is 33⅓% above cost.

questions.q: Successive discounts of 10% and 5% are given on a table marked ₹2000. The price paid is:
questions.e: After 10%: 2000 × 0.9 = 1800. After 5% on that: 1800 × 0.95 = ₹1710. Using 15% on 2000 gives ₹1700, which is wrong.

questions.q: A dishonest shopkeeper sells goods at cost price but uses a weight of 900 g in place of 1 kg. His gain percent is:
questions.e: He gives 900 g and charges for 1000 g. Gain = 100/900 × 100 = 11 1/9%. Dividing by 1000 gives the wrong 10%.

questions.q: A man sells two articles at ₹990 each. On one he gains 10% and on the other he loses 10%. His overall result is:
questions.e: CP of the first = 990 ÷ 1.1 = 900; CP of the second = 990 ÷ 0.9 = 1100. Total CP = 2000, total SP = 1980, so the loss is 20, which is 1%.

questions.q: A sells an article to B at a profit of 20%, and B sells it to C at a profit of 25%. If C pays ₹750, the cost price for A was:
questions.e: 750 = 1.25 × B's price, so B paid 600. Then 600 = 1.2 × A's cost, so A's cost = ₹500.

questions.q: An article marked ₹800 is sold for ₹608 after two successive discounts, the first being 20%. The second discount is:
questions.e: After 20%: 800 × 0.8 = 640. Then 608/640 = 0.95, so the second discount is 5%.

questions.q: A trader marks goods 50% above cost. He then gives successive discounts of 20% and 5%. His profit percent is:
questions.e: Take CP = 100, MP = 150. After 20%: 120; after 5% on that: 120 × 0.95 = 114. Profit = 14%.
